Imagine playing twenty questions to guess an object. A decision tree works similarly, asking simple yes or no questions one by one. For example, 'Is the petal shorter than two point four five centimetres?' or 'Is it wider than one point seven five centimetres?' It keeps asking until it knows the answer.

A single decision tree is easy to understand, but it can be a bit 'jumpy'. Small changes in our data might lead to a completely different tree. It also tends to 'memorise' the training information too well. To fix this, we create a 'committee of trees', combining many trees through voting or averaging their predictions.

The spheres instantly reconfigure: one section has four red and one blue, the other has one red and four blue. An overhead camera with subtle zoom reveals the much cleaner separation. For your exams, remember that increasing 'minimum samples per leaf' reduces overfitting. Ensembles like voting or random forests are powerful, especially 'soft voting' with probabilities. Also, 'feature importances' tell us which factors truly matter. You've learned to build and tame trees, and combine them into smart committees. Great job!
